slots.theme: Problem → solution: the car battery on the first cold morning
slots.caption:
The first really cold morning of the year has a way of finding the weak battery in your driveway.

You turn the key or press the button, and get a slow crank. Or nothing.

Cold weather is hard on car batteries, and it tends to expose the ones that were already tired. The frustrating part is that the warning signs were usually there weeks earlier. The car was due for service, the battery was getting old, the tire pressure light flickered on a chilly morning. It just wasn't written down anywhere you'd see it.

That's the problem with keeping car maintenance in your head while the rest of the house lives on sticky notes.

In Homvi, your car or EV is an asset on the same dashboard as the furnace and the generator. It gets its own service schedule, by date or by mileage, so a battery check or a pre-winter service shows up as due soon before the cold snap, not after it.

Not sure what a winter check should cover? Ask the Homvi AI assistant.

slots.theme: Home tip: outdoor faucets and hoses before the freeze
slots.caption:
The garden hose you left connected in October can crack a pipe behind your wall in December.

When water trapped in a hose freezes, it has nowhere to go but back toward the faucet and the pipe behind it. It's one of the easiest winter problems to prevent, and one of the easiest to forget.

A quick homeowner checklist before the first hard freeze:

1. Disconnect every garden hose, drain it and store it inside.
2. If your outdoor faucets have indoor shut-off valves, close them, then open the outside tap to let it drain.
3. Put an insulated cover on each outdoor spigot.
4. Have an irrigation system? Get the lines drained or blown out before the ground freezes.
5. Store the pressure washer and any other water-filled tools somewhere above freezing.

Frost-free spigots help, but only if the hose is off. Ten minutes now beats a wet basement later.

slots.theme: Feature spotlight: the dashboard and Home Health Score
slots.caption:
Here's a question most homeowners can't answer quickly: is anything in your house overdue right now?

Not broken. Just overdue. The filter you meant to change, the purifier cartridge, the generator test run.

Homvi's dashboard is built to answer that at a glance. At the top is your Home Health Score, one number that sums up every asset you track. Below it are three counts: overdue, due soon and healthy. Then your upcoming tasks, in order.

The moment it's designed for is small. Sunday evening, planning the week. You open the app, see two items in red and three in amber, and you know exactly what deserves an hour on Saturday. Everything green can stay out of your head.

It matters most this time of year, when the furnace, the generator and the HVAC filter all want attention before winter, and the holidays want everything else.

slots.theme: Founder note: AI for the chores, not your attention
slots.caption:
Almost every new app calls itself AI-powered now. The phrase has nearly stopped meaning anything.

So while building Homvi, I've tried to hold myself to one rule: the AI should take over the parts of home maintenance nobody enjoys, and stay out of the way everywhere else.

In practice, that's three jobs.

Reading. You photograph an appliance's nameplate, and Homvi AI fills in the brand, model and specs, so you never type a model number.

Answering. The small questions that come up at 7 a.m., like whether a strange furnace noise can wait, get a plain answer in the assistant chat.

Estimating. Ask what the coming quarter looks like, and the assistant gives you a budget estimate for the maintenance that's due.

What I've left alone matters just as much. Your schedules, reminders and Home Health Score stay simple and predictable. You should always know why something is due.

That's my test for every AI feature before launch: does it remove a chore, or just add a chat window?

Where do you actually want AI in your home, and where would you rather it stayed out?
